edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἵνα δοκῇ καὶ ἄλλους εἰδέναι παρ᾿ οὓς ὠνόμασε, φησὶν ἑαυτῷ συνήθως ὅτι ἄλλοι ἄλλον διδάσκαλόν τε καὶ δαίμονα, κακῶς πλαζόμενοι καὶ καλινδούμενοι κατὰ σκότον πολὺν τῶν Ἀντίνου τοῦ κατ᾿ Αἴγυπτον θιασωτῶν ἀνομώτερόν τε καὶ μιαρώτερον. καὶ δοκεῖ μοι ἐπαφώμενος τῶν πραγμάτων ἀληθές τι εἰρηκέναι, ὅτι τινὲς ἄλλοι ἄλλον δαίμονα κακῶς πλαζόμενοι καὶ καλινδούμενοι εὕραντο προστάτην κατὰ πολὺν τὸν τῆς ἀγνοίας σκότον. περὶ δὲ τῶν κατὰ τὸν Ἀντίνουν, παραβαλλόμενον ἡμῶν τῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων εἰπόντες οὐ παλιλλογήσομεν. καὶ βλασφημοῦσι δὲ, φησὶν, εἰς ἀλλήλους οὗτοι πάνδεινα ῥητὰ καὶ ἄῤῥητα· καὶ οὐκ ἂν εἴξαιεν οὐδὲ καθ᾿ ὁτιοῦν εἰς ὁμόνοιαν, πάντῃ ἀλλήλους ἀποστυγοῦντες. καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα δ᾿ ἡμῖν εἴρηται ὅτι καὶ ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ ἔστιν εὑρεῖν αἱρέσεις αἱρέσεσι πολεμούσας καὶ ἐν ἰατρικῇ. οἱ μέντοι τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀκολουθοῦντες καὶ μεμελετηκότες αὐτοῦ τοὺς λόγους φρονεῖν καὶ λέγειν καὶ ποιεῖν „λοιδορούμενοι εὐλογοῦμεν, διωκόμενοι ἀνεχόμεθα, δυσφημούμενοι παρακαλοῦμεν·“ καὶ οὐκ ἂν ῥητὰ καὶ ἄῤῥητα λέγοιμεν τοὺς ἄλλα δοξάζοντας παρ᾿ ἃ ὑπειλήφαμεν· ἀλλ᾿, εἰ μὲν δυνάμεθα, πάντα ἂν πράττοιμεν ὑπὲρ τοῦ αὐτοὺς μεταστῆσαι ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον διὰ τοῦ προσανέχειν μόνῳ τῷ δημιουργῷ καὶ πάντα πράττειν ὡς κριθησομένους. εἰ δὲ μὴ πείθοιντο οἱ ἑτερόδοξοι, τηροῦμεν τὸν προστάξαντα αὐτοῖς λόγον τοιαῦτα· „αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον μετὰ μίαν καὶ δευτέραν νουθεσίαν παραιτοῦ, εἰδὼς ὅτι ἐξέστραπται ὁ τοιοῦτος καὶ ἁμαρτάνει ὢν αὐτοκατάκριτος.“ ἔτι δὲ (οἱ) τὸ „μακάριοι οἱ εἰρηνοποιοὶ“ νοήσαντες καὶ τὸ „μακάριοι οἱ πρᾳεῖς“ οὐκ ἂν ἀποστυγήσαιεν τοὺς παραχαράττοντας τὰ χριστιανισμοῦ οὐδὲ Κίρκας καὶ κύκηθρα αἱμύλα λέγοιεν τοὺς πεπλανημένους.
pass_a_gloss: Then so that he may seem to know also others besides those he named, he says in his customary way: [Celsus:] others [follow] another teacher and demon, wandering badly and rolling about in much darkness, more lawless and more foul than the thiasos-members of Antinous in Egypt. [Origen:] And he seems to me, touching on the facts, to have said something true: that some, others another demon, wandering badly and rolling about, found a patron in the much darkness of ignorance. About the [matters] of Antinous, compared with our Jesus, having spoken in the [books] before these we will not repeat. [Celsus:] And these blaspheme, he says, against one another terrible things sayable and unsayable; and they would not yield in anything at all toward concord, loathing one another utterly. [Origen:] To these too it has been said by us that also in philosophy one can find sects warring with sects, and in medicine. Those however following the word of Jesus and having practised to think and say and do his words: 'reviled we bless, persecuted we endure, defamed we exhort/entreat' [1 Cor 4:12-13]; and we would not say things sayable and unsayable [of] those holding other opinions than what we have received/supposed; but, if we are able, we would do all for transferring them to the better through attending to the Creator alone and doing all as about to be judged. But if the heterodox are not persuaded, we keep the word that commanded such things for them: 'a heretical man after one and a second admonition decline/avoid, knowing that such a one has been perverted and sins, being self-condemned' [Titus 3:10-11]. Further those having understood 'blessed the peacemakers' [Mt 5:9] and 'blessed the meek' [Mt 5:5] would not loathe those debasing/counterfeiting the [things] of Christianity nor would call those having strayed Circes and wily stirrers.

pass_b_english: Then, so that he may seem to know of others besides those he named, he says, in his usual way, that “some have one teacher and demon and some another, wandering wretchedly and wallowing in deep darkness, more lawless and more foul than the devotees of Antinous in Egypt.” And it seems to me that here, touching on the facts, he has said something true: that some, wandering wretchedly and wallowing in the deep darkness of ignorance, have found themselves one demon as patron, and others another. As for Antinous, who is compared with our Jesus, we have spoken of him before and will not repeat ourselves.

“And these people,” he says, “hurl at one another every dreadful blasphemy, speakable and unspeakable; and they would not give way in the least toward concord, since they utterly loathe one another.” To this too we have already given our answer: in philosophy as well one can find sects at war with sects, and in medicine also.

We, however, who follow the word of Jesus and have trained ourselves to think and speak and act by his words, “when reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat” (1 Corinthians 4:12–13). Nor would we say things speakable and unspeakable against those whose opinions differ from what we hold. Rather, if we can, we would do everything to bring them over to what is better, by their holding fast to the Creator alone and doing everything as people who will be judged. But if those of other opinions are not persuaded, we keep the word that gave such commands about them: “After a first and second admonition, have nothing more to do with a heretic, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned” (Titus 3:10–11).

Further, those who have understood “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9) and “Blessed are the meek” (Matthew 5:5) would not loathe those who debase the things of Christianity, nor would they call those who have gone astray “Circes” and “wily agitators.”
notes: Two Celsus quotations: 'ἄλλοι ἄλλον διδάσκαλόν τε καὶ δαίμονα... θιασωτῶν ἀνομώτερόν τε καὶ μιαρώτερον' and 'βλασφημοῦσι... ἀποστυγοῦντες'. δαίμων is rendered 'demon' in both Celsus's and Origen's mouths to keep Origen's turn of Celsus's word; for Celsus it meant a lesser divine being, for Origen an evil spirit. Origen's agreement repeats Celsus's participles (κακῶς πλαζόμενοι καὶ καλινδούμενοι) and the same English is kept. 'θιασῶται' = members of a cult guild, rendered 'devotees'. Antinous was treated earlier in this work (book 3). 'ῥητὰ καὶ ἄῤῥητα' = everything one may and may not say. 1 Corinthians 4:12-13 is quoted exactly, with δυσφημούμενοι ('slandered'). Titus 3:10-11 is quoted exactly; 'αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον' rendered 'a heretic', the sense Origen gives it in this discussion of sects (in Titus itself it may mean a factious person). The clause 'διὰ τοῦ προσανέχειν μόνῳ τῷ δημιουργῷ καὶ πάντα πράττειν ὡς κριθησομένους' is ambiguous as to subject (the converts or 'we'); taken as describing the better state into which they are brought. Matthew 5:5 ('Blessed are the meek') is 5:5 in English Bibles (some Greek witnesses place it at 5:4). 'Κίρκας καὶ κύκηθρα αἱμύλα' are presumably names Celsus reported Christians using of one another: Circe (Homer's enchantress, Odyssey 10) and 'κύκηθρον' (a stirring-ladle, used of a trouble-maker) with 'αἱμύλος' (wheedling, wily); rendered 'Circes' and 'wily agitators'. No classical citation is given inline since Origen is not quoting a text.
